item.description:

Huge fire erupts near Cairo killing at least 30 peopleByAleks PhillipsPublished26 minutes ago
At least 30 people have been killed and 19 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.
Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and smoke inhalation after the incident, which occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, to the north of the old city centre, on Wednesday evening.
Unverified footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.
Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported the vehicle had overturned, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.
The regional public prosecutor has launched an investigation into the incident and asked that DNA samples be taken from bodies of the dead.
The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, had been travelling along the highway when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, prompting the driver to lose control, Al-Ahram reports, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation.
It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the state-owned newspaper says.
Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, with informal residential areas and often run-down infrastructure making incidents more common, the response to which is often complicated by slow emergency response times and locally improvised rescue efforts, even in the sprawling Egyptian capital.
Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished, as emergency services blocked off entry routes.

item.title: [ABC News World] South Africa's Biovac aims to dramatically increase vaccine production with help from an EU loan
item.description:
South Africa's Biovac aims to dramatically increase vaccine production with help from an EU loan
South African pharmaceutical company Biovac says it aims to dramatically increase its vaccine production by the end of 2028 with help from a 75-million euro loan from the European Union's investment bankByGERALD IMRAY Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 2:54 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
CAPE TOWN, South Africa -- South Africa’s Biovac said Wednesday that a new manufacturing facility aims to dramatically increase African production of vaccines by the end of 2028 to help reduce the continent’s heavy reliance on imported doses.
Africa needs more than 1 billion vaccine doses a year, but only around 1% of them are manufactured on the continent, according to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Biovac, a public-private pharmaceutical company that's part-owned by the South African government, distributes or does end-stage production for vaccines for polio, tuberculosis, tetanus and other diseases.
It's also seeking regulatory approval to start end-to-end production of an oral cholera vaccine by late 2028, company officials said.
It would be the first cholera vaccine manufactured entirely in Africa and only the second vaccine produced end-to-end on the continent, following a yellow fever vaccine produced by Senegal's Pasteur Institute.
Biovac acquired the base technology for its cholera vaccine from the International Vaccine Institute in South Korea, Biovac CEO Morena Makhoana said. He added that the vaccine is currently undergoing clinical trials and the company expects to have initial safety and efficacy data by June.
Biovac plans to upscale its overall vaccine production by building a new manufacturing facility next to its current base in Cape Town with support from the European Union's investment bank.

2 baby meerkats make their debut at Peruvian zoo, spotlighting conservation
A private zoo in Peru has introduced two baby meerkats born in Lima to raise awareness about wildlife conservationByMAURICIO MUÑOZ Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 4:00 PM
LIMA, Peru -- A private zoo in Peru on Wednesday introduced two baby meerkats born in Lima as part of an effort to raise awareness about wildlife conservation and introduce visitors to the African species.
Eduardo Espíritu, a biologist in charge of mammals at NaviFauna, a private zoo and wildlife refuge, said the initiative aims to educate the public about the importance of protecting biodiversity.
Meerkats are small mammals native to southern Africa that dig underground burrows and often stand upright to keep watch for potential threats.
“Meerkats cannot be pets. They are wild animals,” Espíritu said. “We focus on keeping them healthy, and one sign of that is reproduction,” something the zoo has successfully achieved in Lima.
The zoo is home to 15 meerkats, eight of which have been born in Lima since 2025. The other seven arrived from their native Botswana in 2022 through an exchange between zoos, according to NaviFauna.

item.title: [CBS News World] Leaked data shows 490,000 Russian forces have died in Ukraine war
item.description:
More than 490,000 Russian soldiers have died since Vladimir Putin ordered Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, according to leaked Russian government data analyzed by CBS News partner network BBC News. Another organization's analysis of the vast dataset suggests the toll is likely closer to 700,000.
A recent hack by pro-Ukraine groups Belarusian Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow produced the data that was analyzed by the BBC and independent Russian outlet Mediazona. It included more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, according to the British broadcaster.
The data, which includes granular information on the location of deaths in Ukraine and Russian border regions, age ranges, causes of death, and employment and court rulings suggests at least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died during the war so far, according to the BBC. According to Mediazona's analysis, which the outlet said accounted for delays in death registrations, missing records and deaths occurring since the data was leaked, Russia's total military death toll has likely reached around 700,000.
In May, the head of the United Kingdom's communications and cyber spy agency also put the number of Russian military deaths during the war at about 500,000, citing Western intelligence.
"Putin is going backwards on the battlefield, with new intelligence showing that almost half a million Russian soldiers have been killed since the conflict began," Anne Keast-Butler, the director of the Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ), said at the time.
Soldiers carry the coffin of 20-year-old Russian serviceman Nikita Avrov during his funeral at a church in Luga, south of St. Petersburg, April 11, 2022, after his death during the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine.

A fire on a major highway surrounding Cairo kills at least 30 people, Egypt’s Health Ministry says
Egypt’s Health Ministry says a fire broke out on a major highway surrounding Cairo, leaving at least 30 people deadByThe Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 2:14 PM
Share
CAIRO -- A fire broke out on a major highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, leaving at least 30 people dead, Egypt’s Health Ministry said.
The cause of the blaze was not immediately known. The ministry said that in addition to those killed, at least 15 people were injured in the fire on Ring Road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital.
At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video shows firefighters working to put out the fire spreading amongst the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb.
Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement.
Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the 15 injured were taken to nearby hospital and that he would head to the scene himself.

item.title: [BBC World] Images of asteroid targeted to test Earth's defences reveal stadium-sized crater
item.description:
Image source, ESAImage caption,
The asteroid before (left) and after, showing the crater left behind by a spacecraft's impactByRebecca Morelle, Alison Francis and Tony Jolliffe, BBC science teamPublished25 November 2026, 06:00 GMTUpdated 4 hours ago
The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface.
The extensive damage was caused when a Nasa spacecraft hit the asteroid Dimorphos in 2022. The asteroid posed no threat, but this was a test of our planetary defences to see if it was possible to knock a space rock off course.
Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision.
"The crater is almost as large as the body itself, which is really, really spectacular," said Dr Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist, who is on the Hera science team.
"It's hard to describe in words all the excitement to actually finally see what happened. And as a crater person, I can also say it's beautiful."
The original 2022 crash test was carried out by a Nasa spacecraft called Dart which hurtled into Dimorphos at 14,000mph (22,000km/h).
It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 6,200 miles long (10,000km), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.
Dimorphos is about 150m (500ft) wide and was partly chosen as the target because it is one of an asteroid pair - it orbits around a larger space rock called Didymos, which is about 730m (2,400ft) wide.
The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.
Before the collision, it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.

Watch: What we know about Trump's Thanksgiving tariffsByMichael Race and Jonathan Josephs, Business reportersPublished25 November 2026, 00:38 GMTUpdated 5 hours ago
The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.
The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions.
The move follows the White House's investigation into the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.
China is facing the highest rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35% and then others facing either 20% or 25%.
The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year.
Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of the good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing the products from abroad.
Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.
The proposed tariffs will affect China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy".
He claimed that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression" as well as "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America's manufacturing base".

Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.
"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."
Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.
"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."
The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. item.title: [BBC China] Xi's anti-corruption campaign ensnares rising star in Chinese Communist Party
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Chen Jining was a rising star in the Chinese Communist PartyByKoh EwePublished25 November 2026, 05:37 GMT
Chinese authorities are investigating Shanghai's party chief, a rising star in the Communist Party, as part of Xi Jinping's sweeping anti-corruption drive.
Chen Jining, 62, is suspected of "severe violations of discipline and laws", according to a statement published on Tuesday by the party's anti-corruption body.
Chen is now the fourth member of the elite Politburo to be investigated, in the widest purge yet of the party's top executive body since the end of the Cultural Revolution.
As the party prepares to appoint fresh leaders at next year's National People's Congress, uncertainty looms over what its new command will look like - except that Xi will remain at the helm.
Before Chen, three other members of the current Politburo - appointed in 2022 - were investigated and subsequently expelled: ex-generals He Weidong and Zhang Youxia, as well as former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui.
While Chen has not been removed from the Politburo, it's rare for officials to return after such investigations.
"Who on this Politburo feels safe, especially as the personnel machinations for next year's Party Congress intensify?" China analyst Bill Bishop wrote in his Sinocism newsletter.
Chen's investigation came as a surprise, according to Bishop, given rumours were swirling that another senior official, not Chen, would fall next in the anti-corruption campaign.
The role of Shanghai party chief, which Chen assumed in 2022, is known to be a prestigious springboard to the country's top office.
Chen's long list of predecessors include former president Jiang Zemin, his premier Zhu Rongji, incumbent premier Li Qiang and Xi Jinping himself.

item.title: [BBC China] What Jensen Huang's return teaches China's Xi about Trump
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to NvidiaByLaura BickerChina correspondent Published24 November 2026
Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform.
Most users are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets.
But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China.
That's probably how Xi Jinping sees it too.
Beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt".
Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing.
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Trunmp and Xi ahead of their meeting in Shenzhen last week
Xi will have learned many lessons from this scandal, especially about Trump's pressure points.
For one, the fact that Huang's reappointment came so soon after Xi's meetings last week with Trump in Shenzhen could be read as a sign that direct engagement is an effective way to influence Washington.
